extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of experimental natural philosophy / history and philosophy of science (readers of Bacon and experimental-method instruction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, measuring, and interpreting experiments in natural philosophy (Baconian experimental method): which kinds of instances to collect, how to measure and compare effects in time and quantity, how to set up contests of opposing causes. Emphasises quantification, comparative measurement, sequencing, doses, and classification of competing motions/virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to law and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations and experimental results should be reduced to law and measurement; quantification is the merit of sound research (e.g., Boyle and others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states 'is the reduction of them to law and measurement which has constituted the merit of the researches of Boyle and others.' Practical guidance: prefer experiments that yield measurable quantities and laws rather than merely qualitative reports; use instruments (piezometer, clocks, etc.) to obtain quantitative data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Curriculi (Instantiae ad Aquam) — measure by moments of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect 'instances' that measure nature by moments of time (instantiae curriculi / ad aquam): every natural motion or action is transacted in time and should be measured in temporal moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use instruments and methods that provide temporal measurement (dials, pendulums, clocks, chronometers, transit instruments) and methods for computing velocities (sound, light, electricity). Examples and suggested experiments: comparing times of seeing a light vs hearing a sound to determine speed of sound; use of personal equation in observatories. Instruments explicitly cited: dial, pendulum, clock, watch, chronometer, electric clock, transit instrument. Emphasises that even apparently instantaneous actions have measurable temporal structure and should be probed by time-measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative measurement (mensurae comparativae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure phenomena comparatively rather than only simply: comparisons reveal differences of rate, persistence, and relative effect (e.g., light vs sound, visual persistence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comparative approach is 'multo magis' useful; examples include: flame seen before sound is heard, persistence of retinal images causing apparent multiplicity of vibrating strings or rotating rings, and differences in velocities (light vs sound). Comparative measures expose unequal motions and should be used to infer causes (Galileo's use noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primo et Posterius — note sequence and temporal phases of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish and record the earlier (prima) and later (posterius) effects in any natural action; initial and later effects may be qualitatively different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: infusion of rhubarb gives purgative force first and astringent later; infusion of violets yields a delicate odour initially and a more earthy part later; distillation of macerated aromatics yields first aqueous phlegm, then spirit-wine fraction, then aromatic fraction. Experimental design should sample at multiple timepoints and consider renewing material (e.g., repeated short infusions) to optimize desired effects. Note: aroma may not reach full strength until a month after infusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Quanti / Doses Naturae — measure virtue by quantity (dose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect instances that measure virtues/effects by the quantity of material (doses): determine what quantity of a body produces a given effect and how quantity modulates virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes medical 'doses' and chemical proportions (law of definite proportions given as relevant). Guidance emphasises that some virtues only exist at cosmic quantities or change with scale; many particular virtues operate according to the magnitude of the body. Examples: waters in large vs small masses behave differently (sea vs rivers), must/ale mature faster in small vessels, infusion vs imbibition depending on herb proportion, small droplets in air dissipate rather than fall. Empirical measurement of dose-response is required; avoid assuming simple proportional scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative ratios do not equal ratios of virtue (nonlinearity of scaling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that doubling quantity yields double effect; ratios of quantity do not straightforwardly correspond to ratios of virtue or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warns against naive proportional reasoning (example: heavier lead ball does not fall twice as fast). 'Itaque hae mensurae ex rebus ipsis petendae sunt, et non ex verisimilitudine aut conjecturis' — measure from the things themselves, not from conjecture or simple analogy. Experimental designs should test scaling relations empirically rather than infer them from arithmetic proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions re: Niimis et Parum (too much and too little)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always note cautions about excesses and insufficiencies; small and large quantities may produce qualitatively different outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises attention to 'Niimis et Parum aspergendae' when treating dose and quantity. Examples: small drops in the air never fall but dissipate; a small fragment of magnet does not attract as much as the whole magnet. Design experiments to probe extremes (very small and very large) and document thresholds and qualitative changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Luctae (Instances of Lucta / Predominance) — set up contests of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect 'wrestling instances' that show predominance and yielding among virtues/motions by pitting them against each other; identify which virtue is stronger in specific conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose and compare primary species of motion/virtue to make comparisons of strength: set up experiments where two candidate causes compete and observe which prevails. The method requires specifying the species of motion involved and designing experiments of conflict (e.g., blasting where expansion motion overcomes gravity/inertia). Use the outcomes to define and designate 'instantiae luctae' and to infer comparative strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify primary species of motion (motus) to structure comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing virtues/causes, first enumerate and define the principal kinds of motion/virtue (Motus Primus, Secundus, Tertius, etc.) to make comparisons perspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives examples of classes: Motus Primus (motus antitypiae materiae — indestructibility/incompressibility aspect), Motus Secundus (nexus — cohesion/no vacuum; examples: suction by pumps, ventosas), Motus Tertius (liberation — bodies freeing themselves from pressure). Guidance: use these classificatory lenses when designing 'luctae' experiments; the commentary notes Bacon's usage of 'motion' is broad and sometimes vague, so modern experimenters should clarify definitions before testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empiricism over analogy and conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer measurements and mensurae 'ex rebus ipsis' (from the things themselves) rather than relying on verisimilitude, analogy, or conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author admonishes that measures must be sought from the things themselves and not from likelihood or conjectures. Anti-patterns: drawing conclusions from mere analogy (e.g., assuming mathematical proportionality across different virtues) or from purely speculative reasoning without experimental verification.
